name: Paro Tshechu
when: March or April (10th to 15th day of the 2nd Bhutanese lunar month)
summary: Paro Tshechu is a five-day spring festival of masked dances at Rinpung Dzong, ending at dawn on the last day with the unveiling of a giant thongdrel, a sacred appliqué image of Guru Rinpoche. It is one of the two largest Tshechus in Bhutan.
body: Tshechu means the tenth day, the day of the lunar month associated with Guru Rinpoche. Paro's festival is held in the courtyard of Rinpung Dzong and then in the large open ground below it. Monks and laymen in silk costumes and carved masks perform cham dances that tell stories of Guru Rinpoche, the defeat of evil and the judgement of the dead. Clowns called atsaras move among the crowd with jokes.

Families come in their best gho and kira, carrying picnics, and the festival is as much a social event as a religious one. Before sunrise on the final day the thongdrel, a vast thangka several storeys high, is unrolled on the dzong wall for a few hours. Seeing it is believed to bring merit, and crowds gather in the dark to wait.
tips: Book Paro hotels three to four months ahead; festival week fills fast.
Reach the dzong before 4 am on the last day to see the thongdrel unveiled.
Wear long sleeves and trousers or a long skirt; formal dress is appreciated.
Do not use flash or walk into the dance ground for photographs.
Exact dates follow the lunar calendar and change each year. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: From the 10th to the 15th day of the second month of the Bhutanese lunar calendar, which usually falls in late March or April. Dates change every year. The Department of Tourism publishes the festival calendar in advance. Check current status before you travel and book hotels early.

faqs.q: What is the thongdrel at Paro Tshechu?
faqs.a: A huge religious appliqué image, several storeys high, of Guru Rinpoche and his companions. It is unrolled on the wall above the festival ground before dawn on the last day and taken down before the sun strikes it. Seeing it is believed to cleanse sins and bring merit.

Yes. Tourists are welcome with a licensed guide, though in Paro you do not strictly need one. There is no separate ticket in most years, but rules can change. Dress modestly, stay behind the dance area, do not use flash and keep quiet during the religious dances.

Yes, especially on the final day for the thongdrel. Thousands of Bhutanese and visitors gather in the festival ground. Arrive early for a good spot, keep your belongings close and be patient leaving. Hotels and cars in Paro and Thimphu are booked out, so plan months ahead.

name: Thimphu Tshechu
when: September or October (10th to 12th day of the 8th Bhutanese lunar month)
summary: Thimphu Tshechu is the capital's three-day autumn festival of masked dances, held at Tashichho Dzong and the festival ground beside it. It draws the biggest crowds of any festival in Bhutan.
body: The festival is preceded by days of prayer inside Tashichho Dzong, and the public dances take place over three days in the Tendrelthang festival ground beside it. Monks and laymen perform the cham dances in carved masks and silk robes, including the Black Hat dance, the dance of the stags and hounds, and dances of the eight manifestations of Guru Rinpoche.

People from across the country come dressed in their finest clothes, and the event mixes devotion, family picnics and catching up with friends. A thongdrel is displayed at dawn on the final day. October is also the clearest month in the mountains, so the festival fits well with a trip to Punakha and Paro.
tips: Book Thimphu hotels at least three months ahead; prices rise in festival week.
Go early on each day to get a seat on the steps around the festival ground.
Carry a cushion, water, sunscreen and a warm layer for the evenings.
Combine the festival with Dochula and Punakha, which are clear in October.
Dates change each year with the lunar calendar. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: The public festival runs for three days from the 10th day of the eighth Bhutanese lunar month, usually in late September or October. Prayers and preparations begin several days earlier inside Tashichho Dzong. Dates change every year; the Department of Tourism publishes them in advance. Check current status before you travel.

At the Tendrelthang festival ground beside Tashichho Dzong, on the northern side of the city. Spectators sit on steps around the ground. It is about 10 minutes by car from the city centre. Roads nearby are closed or busy during the festival, so allow extra time.

faqs.q: How long should I stay for Thimphu Tshechu?
faqs.a: One full day is enough to see a good range of dances. Two days lets you watch at a slower pace and see different dances. If you want the thongdrel, plan to be there before dawn on the final day. Fit the rest of your trip around it with Punakha and Paro.

faqs.q: Is Thimphu Tshechu suitable for families?
faqs.a: Yes. The festival is a family event for Bhutanese, and children enjoy the masks, music and clowns. Crowds are heavy, so keep children close and agree a meeting point. Bring snacks, water and sun protection, and be ready for long periods of sitting.

name: Black-necked Crane Festival
summary: The Black-necked Crane Festival is a one-day community festival in the courtyard of Gangtey Goenpa in Phobjikha that celebrates the return of the cranes for the winter. It mixes crane dances by schoolchildren, folk songs and masked dances with conservation messages.
body: The festival is held on 11 November, which is also the birth anniversary of the fourth king. It was started to raise awareness of crane conservation and to tie the local community's pride to the birds' protection. Local schoolchildren in crane costumes perform dances imitating the birds, and villagers perform folk songs and dances.

It is small and informal compared with the Tshechus. Visitors sit with villagers around the courtyard, and the setting, with the valley and the cranes below, is the real draw. Combine it with crane watching at dawn and dusk and a walk on the Gangtey nature trail.
tips: Book Phobjikha rooms two to three months ahead for 11 November.
Dress warmly; mornings in the monastery courtyard are below freezing.
Stay at least two nights so you can watch the cranes before and after.
Keep well back from the cranes in the valley and follow your guide's directions.
Check current status before you travel; festival arrangements can change.

faqs.q: When is the Black-necked Crane Festival in Bhutan?
faqs.a: It is held on 11 November each year at Gangtey Goenpa in the Phobjikha valley, coinciding with the birth anniversary of the fourth king. It lasts one day. Check current status before you travel, as arrangements can change and the date may be adjusted in some years.

faqs.q: What happens at the Black-necked Crane Festival?
faqs.a: Local schoolchildren perform crane dances in costume, villagers perform folk songs and masked dances, and there are short talks and displays on crane conservation. It is a community event focused on the birds and the valley rather than a large religious Tshechu.

faqs.q: Will I see cranes during the festival?
faqs.a: Very likely. By 11 November most of the cranes have usually arrived in Phobjikha. Watch them at dawn and dusk from the valley roads and the crane information centre. Numbers vary from year to year with the weather and conditions on their summer grounds.

faqs.q: How do I get to the Crane Festival?
faqs.a: Travel to Phobjikha with your licensed guide and a route permit for Wangdue Phodrang district, usually from Punakha, about 3 hours away. Stay in the valley the night before, as the festival starts in the morning. Book accommodation well ahead, as rooms are limited.
